Female Goldflag jobfish attain a maximum recorded total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' status as a moderately large-bodied lutjanid inhabiting the deep slopes of oceanic islands. This ultimate length is achieved gradually over a long lifespan, with individuals estimated to live for up to 40 years [am = up to 40 years] under the stable thermal conditions of their mesophotic habitat, where water temperatures average 14.9 °C [T = 14.9 °C]. The extended longevity of this species is typical of many deep-water snappers, which tend to exhibit slow growth rates and delayed maturation compared to their shallower-water congeners. Field surveys conducted across the Pacific indicate that such a prolonged life history strategy is closely linked to the relatively low and consistent productivity of the deep-reef environment, which favors sustained somatic investment over rapid turnover. The trade-off between lifespan and reproductive output becomes evident when considering that females must allocate resources to both structural growth and gamete production over several decades, a pattern that constrains the species' demographic resilience under fishing pressure.

The corresponding body mass at this stage, derived from length-weight relationships for the species, indicates that females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic demands of oocyte production. This early maturation strategy stands in contrast to some other deep-water lutjanids, which delay reproduction until reaching a larger proportion of their asymptotic size, likely reflecting differences in mortality regimes and food availability among habitats.

The age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization to eclosion, is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] when eggs are incubated at a stable water temperature of 14.9 °C [T = 14.9 °C]. This rapid embryonic development is typical of tropical and subtropical marine fishes, where warm ambient temperatures accelerate cleavage, gastrulation, and organogenesis, allowing the prolarvae to hatch and enter the planktonic environment quickly. The timing of hatching is critical for matching larval emergence with pulses of planktonic prey, and deviations in incubation temperature can significantly alter survival prospects during this vulnerable early life stage.

Female Goldflag jobfish reach their ultimate somatic size at a wet weight of 1113 grams [Wwi = 1113 grams], a value that corresponds closely to the asymptotic mass predicted by their maximum total length of 45 centimeters. This adult body mass represents the culmination of a slow, steady growth trajectory that extends over many years, during which the fish accumulate substantial lipid reserves in their musculature and viscera. The energy investment required to reach 1113 grams is substantial, and field studies suggest that individuals in regions with lower prey densities may fall short of this asymptotic mass, exhibiting stunted growth curves that reflect resource limitation. This body size also determines the species' reproductive potential, as larger females are capable of producing more and larger eggs, thereby contributing disproportionately to population recruitment in favorable years.

The species' iteroparous strategy, characterized by repeated spawning events across multiple years, is a logical corollary of its long lifespan, as the cumulative reproductive output of a single female over her 40-year lifetime (40 years) [am = 40 years] can amount to tens of millions of eggs at a temperature of 14.9 °C [T = 14.9 °C]. This bet-hedging approach, in which reproductive effort is distributed temporally, buffers the population against stochastic environmental fluctuations, ensuring that recruitment success is not entirely dependent on a single year's conditions.
